entry: European great power conflict, 1701–1714. The death of [[Charles II of Spain|Charles II]] in November 1700, without children, produced a succession crisis between Philip of Anjou, named in Charles's will and backed by [[Louis XIV]] of France, and Charles of Austria, backed by the Second Grand Alliance. Because the [[Spanish Empire]] remained a global power, its acquisition by France or Austria threatened the European balance of power. By 1709 Philip had secured his position in Spain, and when Charles became Holy Roman emperor in 1711, Britain began negotiating its withdrawal. The allies accepted the Peace of Utrecht (1713) and the treaties of Rastatt and Baden (1714). Philip kept the Spanish throne but renounced his rights to the French succession, and Britain gained [[Gibraltar]] and Menorca, replacing the Dutch Republic as the leading naval power. For France, a Bourbon on the Spanish throne broke the Habsburg encirclement of its borders.

Global military campaign launched by the United States after the September 11 attacks. It initially targeted [[Al-Qaeda]] and the Taliban, with its main theater in Afghanistan and Pakistan, and later included the Ba'athist regime in [[Iraq]], deposed in a 2003 invasion, and the [[Islamic State]], which emerged as a key adversary after 2014. [[George W. Bush]] first used the term in September 2001, and it was criticized from the start, prompting the administration to adopt more nuanced terms. According to the Costs of War Project, the post-9/11 wars displaced 38 million people and caused more than 4.5 million deaths, at a cost of over $8 trillion to the U.S. Treasury. Critics have argued that the campaign infringed on [[Civil liberties]], and practices including [[Torture]], drone warfare and extraordinary rendition have been condemned. Security analysts contend that terrorism is not an identifiable enemy and that no military solution exists.

Building for storing goods, usually large and plain and often sited in industrial parks. Warehouses usually have loading docks for trucks, and sometimes receive goods directly from railways, airports or seaports. [[Crane (machine)|Cranes]] and forklifts move goods, which are typically stored on ISO standard pallets in pallet racks. In India and Hong Kong a warehouse is called a godown. In ancient Rome the horreum was a standard building form, and the Horrea Galbae at Ostia had 140 rooms on its ground floor alone, covering about 225,000 square feet (21,000 m²). From the [[Middle Ages]] warehouses were built around ports, and the [[Industrial Revolution]] brought larger, specialized facilities near canals and railways. Warehouses remain a link in [[Logistics|logistics]] and supply chains between production and delivery to end users, and the timber warehouses of Bergen's Bryggen are a [[World Heritage Site]].

Science fiction miniature wargame produced by the British company Games Workshop. Players fight battles on a tabletop with miniature models, resolving combat with [[Dice]] and simple [[Arithmetic|arithmetic]]. It is the most popular miniature wargame in the world. Set in the distant future, its stagnant human civilization is beset by aliens and supernatural creatures. The setting has inspired many novels, role-playing games and video games, and is considered foundational to the grimdark genre of speculative fiction.

Pre-Inca civilization of the south-central [[Andes]], c. AD 500–1000. The Wari, whose former capital lay near modern Ayacucho, [[Peru]], formed an empire that dominated much of the highlands and coast. Its expansion, possibly driven by religious conversion, agricultural knowledge or conquest, brought much of the territory of the earlier Moche and later Chimu cultures under its control. The Wari introduced terrace agriculture in the Carahuarazo Valley, shifting staple crops toward [[Maize|maize]]. Although little is known of their administration, many scholars believe the khipu, a system of knotted cords, was first used as a recording device in Wari. Ancestor worship may have been influenced by the contemporary [[Tiwanaku]] culture. As drought set in around 800, the state declined, and the city of Wari was largely depopulated by 1000. Its roads and governing traditions later shaped the Inca Empire, which followed about 500 years later.

American film studio and distribution arm of Warner Bros. Entertainment. Founded on April 4, 1923, by the Warner brothers, it is the third-oldest film studio in the United States still operating, after [[Paramount Pictures]] and [[Universal Pictures]]. Its first sound film, *The Jazz Singer* (1927), was a landmark. Major franchises include *Superman*, *Harry Potter* and *Batman*. In November 1966 [[Jack L. Warner]] sold 32% of control of the studio and its music business to Seven Arts Productions for $32 million. In 2025 parent Warner Bros. Discovery announced plans to split into two companies.

American actor and filmmaker, a pioneer of the [[New Hollywood]] movement. He made his acting debut in [[Elia Kazan]]'s *Splendor in the Grass* (1961), and his starring roles include *Bonnie and Clyde* (1967) and *Shampoo* (1975). He won the Academy Award for Best Director for *Reds* (1981) and has received 14 nominations from the [[Academy Awards]] overall. He also directed and starred in *Dick Tracy* (1990) and *Bulworth* (1998). A longtime [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] supporter, he campaigned for Robert F. Kennedy in 1968 and George McGovern in 1972. His sister is the actress [[Shirley MacLaine]].

American investor and philanthropist, chairman emeritus of [[Berkshire Hathaway]]. Buffett grew up in [[Omaha, Nebraska|Omaha]], the son of a U.S. congressman, and as a boy sold chewing gum, Coca-Cola and magazines door to door. He studied at the Wharton School of the [[University of Pennsylvania]] and at Columbia Business School, where he adopted the value investing approach of Benjamin Graham. He formed Buffett Partnership in 1956, and his investment firm later acquired the textile maker Berkshire Hathaway, which he led from 1970. He is one of the best-known investors in the world, with an estimated net worth of US$148.9 billion according to [[Forbes]] in January 2026. Buffett has pledged to give away 99 percent of his fortune and co-founded The Giving Pledge in 2010 with [[Bill Gates]] and Melinda French Gates.

Period of Chinese history, c. 475–221 BC. It comprises the final centuries of the [[Zhou dynasty]] (c. 1046–256 BC), when the Zhou king formally ruled but functioned as a figurehead. Sima Qian's choice of 475 BC as its start is the most often cited, and the name comes from the Record of the Warring States, a history compiled in the early Han dynasty. Seven major states, including Qin, Chu and Qi, fought hundreds of wars between 535 and 286 BC, bringing warfare, bureaucratic and military reform and new weapons such as the [[Crossbow]] and improved [[Siege|siege]] engines. Qin annexed each rival by 221 BC and founded the [[Qin dynasty]], the first imperial dynastic state in East Asian history. The era also saw major philosophical development, including [[Mencius]] and Xunzi's refinements of Confucianism.

Series of civil wars in England, 1455–1487. The conflict pitted the Yorkist and Lancastrian branches of the [[House of Plantagenet]] against each other for the English throne, and was rooted in economic strain from the [[Hundred Years' War]] and in [[Feudalism|bastard feudalism]], the private retinues of powerful nobles. Fighting began in 1455 at the First Battle of St Albans, where the Yorkists captured Henry VI. [[Edward IV]], a Yorkist, took the throne in 1461 after defeating the Lancastrians at Towton, the bloodiest battle of the wars. After Edward's death in 1483 his brother Richard III seized the throne, and Henry Tudor, a Lancastrian claimant, defeated and killed him at Bosworth Field in 1485. Henry VII then married Elizabeth of York, Edward IV's daughter, to unite the rival houses, and the last Yorkist resistance was crushed at Stoke Field in 1487. The [[House of Tudor|Tudor]] dynasty ruled until 1603. The name, referring to the rival rose badges, was not used by contemporaries and became common in the early 19th century.

Military alliance of the [[Eastern Bloc]] led by the [[Soviet Union]], 1955–1991. The Warsaw Pact, formally the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance, was signed in [[Warsaw]] in May 1955 as the military complement to the Comecon economic organization and a counterweight to [[NATO]]. The two blocs expanded their forces, but their rivalry was waged through ideology and proxy wars rather than direct confrontation. The pact's largest engagement was the August 1968 invasion of [[Czechoslovakia]], one of its own members, in which all members took part except [[Albania]] and Romania; Albania withdrew less than a month later. The pact began to unravel with the [[Revolutions of 1989]], and East Germany left after German reunification in 1990. On February 25, 1991, the pact ceased to exist, and the Soviet Union itself was dissolved in December 1991.

Capital and most populous city of [[Poland]]. Warsaw stands on the [[Vistula]] river in east-central Poland, with an officially estimated 1.87 million residents in the city and about 3.5 million in its metropolitan area. It became the seat of the Duchy of Masovia in 1413, and in 1596 Sigismund III moved the royal court from [[Kraków]] to the city. It remained the capital of the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]] until 1795. Bombed at the start of [[World War II]] in 1939, the historic city was largely destroyed by the 1943 Ghetto Uprising, the 1944 Warsaw Uprising and systematic razing. Its reconstructed Old Town became a [[World Heritage Site]] in 1980. The city is a major financial center, and its [[Stock exchange|stock exchange]] is the largest in Central and Eastern Europe.

Naval ship built and used primarily for naval warfare. Usually operated by a [[Navy]], warships are armed, designed to withstand damage and typically faster and more maneuverable than [[Merchant ship|merchant ships]], which carry cargo. Unlike merchant ships, they carry only weapons, ammunition and supplies for their crews. Until the 17th century merchant ships were routinely pressed into naval service, and until piracy declined in the 19th century, larger merchant ships such as galleons were commonly armed. In wartime since the early 20th century, merchant ships have also served as auxiliary warships, such as the Q-ships of [[World War I]]. The main types today, in decreasing size, are aircraft carriers, amphibious assault ships, cruisers, [[Destroyer|destroyers]], [[Frigate|frigates]], corvettes and fast attack boats. Modern submarines can remain underwater for months.

Non-cancerous viral growth, usually on the hands or feet, caused by the human papillomavirus. The virus typically enters through a [[Wound|skin wound]]. Without treatment most warts resolve within months to years, and treatments such as [[Salicylic acid]] and [[Liquid nitrogen|cryotherapy]] may speed resolution. Common types include plantar warts on the soles of the feet and genital warts, which are often sexually transmitted. Warts are common, with an estimated 1–13% of the general population affected by non-genital warts, more often in young people. They have been described since 400 BC, when [[Hippocrates]] wrote of them.

Species of edible plant in the family [[Brassicaceae]], also called Japanese horseradish (*Eutrema japonicum*). It grows naturally along stream beds in mountain valleys in Japan, the Russian Far East and the Korean Peninsula. Its rhizome is ground into a pungent paste eaten with [[Sushi]]. Its heat stimulates the nose more than the tongue, similar to [[Horseradish]] or [[Mustard (condiment)|hot mustard]] rather than chili peppers. The oldest record of wasabi as food dates to the 8th century. Because the true plant is difficult to cultivate on a large scale, western horseradish is widely used in its place outside Japan.

Home appliance designed to launder clothing, usually with water. Before washing machines and indoor plumbing, laundry was washed by hand in a process that often occupied a whole day, including carrying water, soaking, scrubbing and wringing. The first English patent for a washing machine was issued in 1691, and a rotating drum washer was patented in 1782. Electric machines were advertised as early as 1904, and the first automatic washing machine was introduced in 1937. Modern machines fill with water, agitate or tumble the laundry with [[Detergent|detergent]], then drain, rinse and spin. The spread of washing machines has been linked to improvements in women's position in society. Irish feminist Mary Frances McDonald called it the most life-changing invention for women, and Swedish statistician Hans Rosling called it the greatest invention of the [[Industrial Revolution]]. The global market was valued at about $63 billion in 2024.

Federal district and capital city of the [[United States]] (pop., 2020: 689,545). Located on the northeast bank of the Potomac River, across from Virginia and surrounded by Maryland, the city was established under the Residence Act of 1790 and designed in 1791 by Pierre Charles L'Enfant. It is named for Columbia, the personification of the nation, and its common name honors [[George Washington]]. The capital moved from [[Philadelphia]] in 1800, when second president [[John Adams]] moved into the newly finished White House. Congress retains power over local law, and residents have no voting representation in Congress, though a locally elected mayor and council have governed the district since 1973. The city hosts the White House, the Capitol and the Supreme Court, and 177 foreign embassies. It is also the headquarters of the [[International Monetary Fund]] and the [[Organization of American States]].

State in the [[Pacific Northwest]] region of the [[United States]], named for [[George Washington]]. Admitted to the Union in 1889 as the 42nd state, it has Olympia as its capital and Seattle as its largest city. With a population of over 8 million, it is the 13th most populous state. Mount Rainier, an active [[Stratovolcano]], is the state's highest point at 14,400 feet (4,389 meters). Washington is the largest U.S. producer of apples, hops, pears and sweet cherries, and ranks third in wine production. The state was one of the first to legalize cannabis and to permit abortion before [[Roe v. Wade]] in 1973.

Insect of the suborder Apocrita that is neither a [[Bee]] nor an [[Ant]]. Wasps do not form a clade, since bees and ants evolved from wasp ancestors. Most species are solitary, and many are parasitoids that lay eggs in or on other insects, making them valuable in [[Horticulture]] for pest control, such as [[Whitefly|whitefly]] in tomatoes. The best-known social wasps, such as [[Yellowjacket|yellowjackets]] and hornets, are eusocial, living in nests with a queen and non-reproducing workers. Wasps first appeared in the Jurassic and have spread to all parts of the world except the polar regions. The largest social wasp is the [[Asian giant hornet]], up to 5 cm (2.0 in) long. Wasps have appeared in literature since Classical times, including [[Aristophanes]]' 422 BC comedy *The Wasps*.

Russian-born painter and art theorist, one of the pioneers of [[Abstract art|abstract art]]. Born in Moscow to a merchant family, he studied law and economics before enrolling at the Munich Academy in 1896. In Munich he co-founded the Der Blaue Reiter group in 1911 and published *Concerning the Spiritual in Art* the same year, arguing that art should convey inner spiritual truths through color and form independent of objective representation. After returning to Russia during [[World War I]] and the [[Russian Revolution]], he worked in cultural organizations before returning to Germany to teach at the [[Bauhaus]] until the Nazis closed it in 1933. He then settled in France, became a French citizen in 1939 and continued his non-objective compositions until his death in Neuilly-sur-Seine.

Processes that manage waste from its generation to final disposal, covering collection, transport, treatment, monitoring and regulation. In high-income countries waste is typically collected from the street and taken to sanitary [[Landfill|landfills]], incinerators or [[Recycling|recycling]] centers. In lower-income countries a large share is stored in open dumps or burned, and by one estimate about a quarter of municipal solid waste is not collected and another quarter is mismanaged. Poor practice pollutes air, water, soil and food. The waste hierarchy prioritizes prevention and reduction, then reuse, recycling and composting, energy recovery and, last, disposal. Landfills generate methane, a potent greenhouse gas, and recovery of plastics is under 10% worldwide. One projection forecasts a 70% rise in global waste by 2050 without policy changes.

Personal timepiece carried or worn by a person, designed to keep steady time despite the wearer's movements. Watches date from the 16th century, when German clockmakers in [[Nuremberg]] made the first wearable timepieces, although the credit given to Peter Henlein as inventor is uncertain. A balance spring, added to the balance wheel in 1657 in a disputed invention by [[Robert Hooke]] and [[Christiaan Huygens]], cut errors from several hours a day to about 10 minutes. In the 1960s the battery-powered [[Quartz|quartz]] watch was invented, and by the 1980s it dominated the market in the quartz revolution, which decimated the [[Switzerland|Swiss]] watch industry. In the 2010s [[Touchscreen|touchscreen]] smartwatches emerged, with functions far beyond timekeeping. Most timekeeping watches use quartz movements, while expensive collectible watches are valued for craftsmanship and mechanical movements.

Comic book series by [[Alan Moore]] and Dave Gibbons, published by [[DC Comics]] in 1986 and 1987. Set in an alternate 1985 where superheroes changed history so that the United States won the [[Vietnam War]] and the [[Watergate scandal]] was never exposed, the story follows retired vigilantes investigating a murder as tensions with the [[Soviet Union]] near nuclear war. It uses a nonlinear structure and a nine-panel grid. Critics acclaimed it, and [[Time (magazine)|Time]] listed it among the best English-language novels since 1923. A 2009 film, sequels and a 2019 HBO continuation followed. Moore has expressed displeasure with the adaptations and sequels.

Series of about 250 oil paintings by [[Claude Monet]]. Monet painted the flower garden at his home in Giverny, France, and the series was the main focus of his output during the last 31 years of his life, many works made while he suffered from cataracts. The series grew from smaller canvases of the late 1890s to large, immersive panels. In 1922 Monet gave 19 panels to the French state, and eight were installed in oval rooms at the Musée de l'Orangerie, which opened to the public on May 16, 1927. The paintings are displayed in museums worldwide, including the [[Metropolitan Museum of Art]], the [[Museum of Modern Art]] and the [[National Gallery]] in London. In June 2014 one work sold at Sotheby's in London for US$54 million.

Chinese novel from the [[Ming dynasty]], one of the Four Great Classical Novels of Chinese literature. Attributed to Shi Nai'an, with possible contributions from Luo Guanzhong, it was among the first works of Chinese fiction written entirely in vernacular Chinese. Set during the [[Song dynasty|Northern Song]] period, it follows 108 outlaws who gather at Mount Liang to rebel against the government. Later they accept amnesty and fight the [[Liao dynasty]] and other rebels, though many meet tragic ends. The novel has been banned many times for its social critique. Its heroes, such as Song Jiang, Wu Song and Lin Chong, appear in later novels, operas and other media, and the critics Li Zhi and Jin Shengtan placed it among the greatest works of genius in Chinese literature.
